audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Chronicles / Divrei Hayamim Aleph Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher genealogies, first-pass restored draft with public-domain scaffold; later witness audit required
audit_status.review_note: Reviewed for military census language, wives and fertility, variant Benjamin lists, Bilhah, Zelophehad's daughters, women as named builders and sisters, cattle-raiding deaths, mourning, and geographic claims.

verses.restored: Sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron—four.

familiar.text: Now the sons of Issachar were, Tola, and Puah, Jashub, and Shimrom, four.

modern.text: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron—four in all.

original.text: וְלִבְנֵ֣י יִשָׂשכָ֗ר תּוֹלָ֧ע וּפוּאָ֛ה ישיב וְשִׁמְר֖וֹן אַרְבָּעָֽה

verses.restored: Sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Samuel, heads of ancestral houses of Tola, mighty warriors in generations; their number in days of David was twenty-two thousand six hundred.

familiar.text: And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father’s house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred.

modern.text: The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, the heads of their families. In the days of David, 22,600 descendants of Tola were numbered in their genealogies as mighty men of valor.

familiar.text: And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men.

modern.text: The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. The sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah. All five of them were chiefs.

modern.text: In addition to them, according to their genealogy, they had 36,000 troops for battle, for they had many wives and children.

modern.text: All these sons of Jediael were heads of their families, mighty men of valor; there were 17,200 fit for battle.

modern.text: Machir took a wife from among the Huppites and Shuppites. The name of his sister was Maacah. Another descendant was named Zelophehad, who had only daughters.

modern.text: Machir’s wife Maacah gave birth to a son, and she named him Peresh. His brother was named Sheresh, and his sons were Ulam and Rekem.

modern.text: And again he slept with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. So he named him Beriah, because tragedy had come upon his house.

translation_notes: Large military counts reflect the Chronicler's administrative and martial interests and may not define communal worth.
Verse 4 links troop growth with many wives and sons; women are not reproductive infrastructure, and family size is not a Divine score.
Benjamin's genealogy differs substantially from Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles 8; textual and compositional audit is required.
Bilhah is remembered as ancestral mother of Naphtali's line; her enslaved/secondary-wife status in Genesis must not be erased.
Zelophehad's daughters carry an important legal tradition about women's inheritance that the brief mention should not obscure.
Ezer and Elead die during an attempted livestock seizure. Their deaths are grieved, but cattle raiding is not morally innocent.
Ephraim's prolonged mourning and communal comfort validate grief rather than demanding rapid spiritual recovery.
Sheerah is explicitly remembered as a builder of towns; women's engineering and civic leadership must not be minimized.
Territorial and town lists are ancient identity maps, not modern deeds.
safety_note: Reject militarism, fertility hierarchy, polygyny apologetics, cattle-raiding romanticism, gender erasure, and modern territorial claims. Center Bilhah, Maacah, Zelophehad's daughters, Hammolecheth, Serah, Shua, Sheerah the builder, and Ephraim's unshamed grief.
